# Bidirectional Markdown ⇄ Jira rich-text sync (Cloud ADF + DC wiki)

## Context / Problem
The Jira reconciler syncs rebar ticket descriptions and comments as **plain text**, so Markdown structure authors write (headings, checklists, code, lists) shows up as literal source in Jira, and rich text authored in Jira reads as noise in rebar. We want each client to receive a native rich representation — **ADF** for Jira Cloud, **wiki markup** for Jira Data Center — without a sync echo loop that would ratchet Jira-specific formatting back into the store or erode content over repeated passes. Validated over the real historical corpus (1,771 tickets / 5,568 bodies) by six de-risking experiments recorded in session log `5eb0-52a3-45f0-43e5`.

## Approach
Two asymmetric codecs behind one state-based echo-safety layer, because the two Jira targets are fundamentally different formats:
- **Cloud = truly bidirectional, lossless.** ADF is structured JSON; `marklas` round-trips Markdown↔ADF at 99.64% fixed-point over the corpus — the structured-typed-node pattern, inherently echo-safe under normalize-both-sides.
- **DC = one-way MD→wiki render, bidirectional SYNC.** Jira wiki is a lossy text markup and no library round-trips rebar's punctuation-dense prose reliably (pandoc's jira reader misparses `->`, ASCII tables, and regex, and provably erodes them one char per pass). So DC renders one way over the units that are structurally safe, passes dangerous units through verbatim, and prevents loops with **state-based echo suppression** using the reconciler's existing per-binding baseline (ADR 0026, `binding_store.py:102`) — NOT codec fixed-point. Genuine human Jira edits are still detected against baseline and pulled back best-effort.

Echo-safety is state-based for both clients; concurrency is last-write-wins over a three-way state (baseline/local/remote) so neither side's changes are ever silently destroyed. State additions obey epic `0303`'s churn discipline (change-gated, fixed-size, never a per-pass timestamp).

## Dependencies / sequencing
This epic must not be claimed until its three in-flight prerequisites close: `0303` (tickets-store growth / committed-state format), `e369` (Jira-family DC seam), `3e73` (Cloud↔DC test parity). These are recorded as `depends_on` links.

## Child responsibilities (decomposition)
- **Cloud ADF codec** — vendor/pin `marklas`; Markdown↔ADF for descriptions and comments; fix the combined strong+strikethrough mark-order oscillator; accept the ~18 transient whitespace canonicalizations via normalize-both-sides. Delivers AC1.
- **DC one-way segmenting renderer** — split body into blocks/list-items, render structurally-safe units to wiki via pinned pandoc, substitute prose arrows on the Markdown BEFORE pandoc, verbatim-wrap ASCII tables in `{noformat}`, pass dangerous units (tables/arrows/HTML/regex) through unchanged, reassemble. Delivers AC2.
- **DC robustness/perf hardening** — bound pandoc's per-field subprocess cost, add a hard timeout with plain-text fallback on pathological input, and satisfy pandoc GPL/SBOM compliance. Delivers AC2 under production constraints.
- **State echo suppression + LWW conflict safety** — reuse the ADR-0026 baseline (observed-after-push canonical form) plus a change-gated inline `rich_sha`; three-way LWW that always flags concurrent conflict; origin-gated outbound so Jira-native constructs survive. Delivers AC3, AC4, AC5.
- **Comment sync (append-only)** — persistent Jira-comment-ID map (replacing body-equality identity); rebar→Jira creation and inbound new-comment mirroring only (no edit/delete sync); descriptions cut over before comments. Delivers the comment portion of AC1/AC2.
- **Live DC harness + cross-repo contract** — extend the existing Docker Jira DC harness to assert rendered-HTML fidelity (not just wiki source), and add a contract test pinning `normalize_rich_text` back-compat for the sibling `agentic-dev-platform` importer. Delivers AC6.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Cloud descriptions and comments sync as ADF and round-trip Markdown↔ADF with no perpetual re-sync over the historical corpus; verified by a corpus idempotence test that asserts convergence (incl. the two known combined-mark bodies).
- [ ] DC descriptions and comments render to wiki for structurally-safe content while remaining echo-safe with zero content erosion over ≥5 repeated passes, including the known ASCII-table ratchet body; verified by a corpus echo-safety test asserting no monotonic length decay.
- [ ] A reconcile pass in which no body changed writes 0 new committed-state entries and no per-pass timestamp attributable to this feature; verified by the git-delta cost harness reproducing the ≤0.07 KB/version stable profile.
- [ ] A concurrent edit on both sides is always detected and flagged rather than silently overwritten; verified by the concurrent-conflict regression test over the corpus (the proven 799/799-detected invariant).
- [ ] A Jira-authored native construct (panel/mention/date) survives a subsequent rebar-originated reconcile pass; verified by an origin-gating test.
- [ ] The end-to-end behavior runs against a live Jira DC instance asserting rendered HTML (via `?expand=renderedFields`), not just wiki source; verified by the extended Docker DC harness CI job.

# GitHub Issues sync — provider parity with the Jira reconciler (de-Jira-ify the bridge)

## Context

Discovered from the export/import design brainstorm (`rule-swamp-pupil`, 2026-06-17). We want GitHub Issues sync at parity with the existing Jira sync: bidirectional, incremental, idempotent, dry-run by default.

**Critical design conclusion from that brainstorm:** GitHub sync must ride the EXISTING reconciler framework (binding store + outbound/inbound differs + applier), NOT the one-shot export/import path. Import is stateless / additive / lossy and would have to rebuild the entire binding/diff/conflict/convergence layer to do sync — the wrong substrate. git-bug's bridges confirm sync is bidirectional + incremental, distinct from bulk import. The one thing export/import leaves behind for this epic is the provider-neutral `--strip-external` association notion shipped by `rule-swamp-pupil`.

## What / Scope

The spine of this work is **generalizing the reconciler**, which is hardcoded to Jira in 6+ places:

- `jira_key` in the binding store (`rebar_reconciler/binding_store.py`) → a `{provider, external_key}` abstraction.
- `jira-` local-id prefix (`inbound_translate.py:105`).
- ADF (Atlassian Document Format) rich-text codec (`adf.py`) → a GitHub Markdown codec.
- per-type/status/priority maps (`outbound_differ.py`, `inbound_translate.py`) → per-provider registries.
- `<!-- rebar:reconciler-echo -->` loop-breaker marker (`inbound_differ.py`).
- `rebar-id:` Jira labels / entity properties used for binding recovery → a GitHub equivalent.

Then add a **GitHub provider**: REST/GraphQL client, auth (token / `gh`), pagination + rate-limit handling, field mapping (state↔status, labels↔tags, assignees, milestone↔?, comments with external-id dedup), and inbound/outbound apply leaves.

## Success Criteria

- A `{provider, external_key}` binding abstraction replaces hardcoded `jira_key`, with Jira refactored onto it and NO behavior regression (existing Jira reconciler tests stay green).
- GitHub provider does bidirectional incremental sync of issues (create/update/status/comments/labels), idempotent across passes, dry-run default, live writes gated by an env flag mirroring `REBAR_MCP_ALLOW_JIRA_SYNC`.
- Conflict resolution + loop-breaker parity with Jira; `session_log` excluded (parity with `EXCLUDED_SYNC_TYPES`).

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] reconciler binding/translate/differ/codec layers generalized to a provider abstraction; Jira migrated onto it with no regression (existing tests green)
- [ ] GitHub provider client: auth, pagination, rate-limit handling (read + write)
- [ ] field mapping GH↔rebar (state/labels/assignees/comments/external-id dedup) + Markdown codec

without reducing our coverage?" Operator later reported real gate times of 41-47 min.

## What the measurements showed
- Critical path was ONE job: `pytest (macos-latest, py3.13)` at 18.6m (run #1823 /
  id 30569775555). Every other job <=8m; without macOS the run finishes in ~8m.
- Within it: setup 0.7m, twelve drift gates ~0.1m, default pytest tier 15.4m, integration 2.0m.
- 7856 tests: ubuntu 5:04 at -n 4 vs macOS 15:21 at -n 3 — a 3x wall gap against a 1.33x vCPU gap.
- Dispatch lag from Gerrit is NOT a factor: change 1052 ps1 uploaded 18:24:36, run created
  18:24:38 (2s), Verified+1 at 18:53:35 = 29.0m, matching GitHub's own run_duration_ms.
- THE BINDING CONSTRAINT: navapbc is on GitHub Free = 20 concurrent jobs / 5 macOS,
  enforced PER ORGANIZATION, shared with every other navapbc repo. A single Verified run
  needs 21 job slots — one run alone cannot fully parallelize. Six changes dispatched within
  10 seconds queued 6.7-8.4m each for a macOS slot. That queue is the 41-47m.
- Peak concurrent macOS jobs observed across 25 sampled jobs: 4, never more.

- **3-way macOS shard.** `fail_under = 70` is enforced PER pytest session, so every shard

  ./.github/workflows/_build-and-test.yml` resolves from the DEFAULT BRANCH under

# State-based echo suppression + LWW conflict safety

## Context / Problem
Because the DC codec is one-way and lossy, loop prevention cannot rely on `decode(encode(x))==x`. Both clients must instead suppress echo by **state**: compare the current Jira value against the last-synced baseline the reconciler already keeps (ADR 0026, `binding_store.py:102`; `_BASELINE_FIELDS` at line 108; `set_baseline` at line 459). We must also not silently destroy either side's edits under concurrency, and any state we add must respect epic `0303`'s churn discipline (a per-pass timestamp there caused the tickets-store bloat this feature must not regress).

## Approach
Drive body sync from a three-way state — `baseline` (last-synced Jira canonical form), `local` (rebar body), `remote` (current Jira value) — normalized through a **compare-only** `norm()` before diffing. Outbound fires only when `local` differs from `baseline` (rebar-originated change); a value equal to `baseline` is our own echo and is skipped. **The baseline is the value OBSERVED AFTER push** — after pushing a changed field, GET it back and store Jira's canonicalized form as the new baseline (one extra GET, only on change) — which neutralizes Jira's own storage canonicalization so a benign re-canonicalization is never mistaken for a human edit. When both `local` and `remote` diverged from `baseline` (concurrent edit), apply last-write-wins to pick the winner but always emit a detectable conflict signal so nothing is silently lost. For the rich layer, store a **change-gated `rich_sha = sha256(rendered_wire)[:16]` (8 bytes) inline** in the binding (proven 0.07 KB/version stable, identical to baseline; a per-pass timestamp was proven to reproduce 0303's 12.62 KB anti-pattern) so a re-render is only pushed when the wire actually changed. `norm()` stays comparison-only and never writes back (a normalizing write would churn git and re-trigger gates); it absorbs only whitespace and pandoc `<!-- -->` list-separator injects — proven to mask 0 real content changes.

## Scope
- `src/rebar/_engine/rebar_reconciler/binding_store.py` — inline change-gated `rich_sha` beside the existing baseline; observed-after-push baseline update.
- `src/rebar/_engine/rebar_reconciler/inbound_fields.py` — compare-only `norm()` and the three-way diff/LWW arbitration.
- `tests/` — echo, conflict, and no-churn tests.

## Testing
- Self-echo: a rebar-originated body change propagates exactly once and a second reconcile pass pushes nothing (0 echo-back).
- Concurrent: both sides edit the same body; the pass records a conflict and applies LWW without discarding the loser silently (regression asserting the 799/799-detected invariant over the corpus sample).
- No-churn: a pass with no body change updates 0 `rich_sha` entries and writes no timestamp; asserted by the git-delta cost harness (≤0.07 KB/version stable).

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Outbound fires only on a rebar-originated change and the baseline stored is the value observed after push; verified by `test_echo_observed_after_push` (a benign Jira re-canonicalization does not re-sync).
- [ ] A concurrent both-sides edit is detected and flagged under LWW with the losing side never silently destroyed; verified by `REDACTED_TOKEN` (799/799 over the corpus sample).
- [ ] The rich layer stores a change-gated inline 8-byte `rich_sha` and no per-pass timestamp, changing 0 entries on a no-op pass; verified by the git-delta cost harness reproducing the ≤0.07 KB/version stable profile.
- [ ] `norm()` is comparison-only (never written back) and masks 0 real content changes; verified by `test_norm_masks_nothing` over the adversarial pair set.

## Context

Parked from the brainstorm on the migration-pattern epic (odd-vortex-elbow). `rebar
doctor` is a full **diagnose-and-heal health command** in the `brew doctor` /
`flutter doctor` family — a superset of the migration/ensure work. It **depends on**
that migration epic: the ensure-registry + version-marker built there become
doctor's auto-heal category. Design it properly once the migration mechanism exists.

Purpose (per the requesting session): diagnose mismatches between observed project
state and the reported migration version/state; re-apply migrations / correct
inconsistencies that can be **reliably** auto-healed; verify config consistency, that
the ticket store isn't corrupt, and that the environment has the dependencies at the
versions rebar needs; and surface detailed troubleshooting + suggested next steps for
anything it cannot safely auto-heal.

## Proposed design (from OSS research)

**Architecture — a registry of check objects.** Each check:
`{ name, category, run() -> {status, message, fix_command?}, is_required, auto_heal? }`.
Run with **crash-isolation** (one check raising must not abort the run — flutter's
`ValidationResult.crash`) and **per-check timeouts** on anything touching
network/auth. Slow checks run last.

**Four check categories:**
1. **migration / ensure drift** (auto-heal) — the ensure-registry from the migration
   epic; observed-state-vs-marker drift; re-applies idempotent ensures. THIS is the
   provably-safe auto-heal class.
2. **store integrity** (report) — reuse fsck's 5 checks (JSON validity, CREATE
   presence, snapshot consistency, orphan events, push-pending). Non-destructive.
3. **config consistency** (advise / selective-heal) — rebar's own config valid +
   coherent; foreign config only flagged, never silently rewritten.
4. **environment & dependencies** (advise) — Python >=3.11, git present, the
   `[agents]` extra + `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` (LLM ops), `acli` (live Jira), pre-commit
   hook wired, and the **"stale global build vs repo venv"** foot-gun called out in
   CLAUDE.local.md (`which rebar` resolves to `.venv/bin/rebar`).

**Diagnose-vs-autoheal rule (converged prior art):** auto-heal a finding ONLY if it is
idempotent + reversible + non-destructive + reliably resolves the state; otherwise
print the exact remediation command + docs link and leave it. rebar's ensures satisfy
this by construction; env/config issues generally do not -> advise.

**Severity + exit contract:** adopt chezmoi's tiers `ok / info / warning / error /
failed` (+ a `healed` result for was-broken-now-fixed). **Exit code keys on the fatal
tier only** — warnings never fail the process (this cures brew doctor's most-cited
flaw). Standard: `0` = clean or warnings-only or all-healed; non-zero = a fatal check
remains after healing. Offer `--check`/`--dry-run` (read-only, exit non-zero if
anything is behind/broken — the terraform `fmt -check` CI-gate pattern) and `--json`
for machine output (test the exit contract; don't let `--json` silently force 0, gh's
bug; don't let an auto-heal reset the failure count, eslint's `--fix` bug).

**Relationship to `upgrade`:** likely `upgrade` = doctor scoped to just the
migration/ensure category (apply pending migrations without the full env/config scan),
or a thin alias — decide when designing.

## Gotchas to design against (ranked, from research)
1. Crying wolf / false positives (brew's reputation) -> severity tiers + ignorable
   non-failing warnings + a per-finding "why this might be fine" note.
2. Wrong exit-code contract (gh#8845 exit-0-on-fail; brew exit-1-on-warning; eslint
   autofix resets exit) -> decide it explicitly and TEST it; gate on fatal only.
3. Network/auth checks that hang (flutter license/proxy; npm ping) -> timeout every
   one; classify timeout distinctly from broken; make them skippable.
4. Non-idempotent/destructive auto-fixes (git `gc --prune=now`; docker `prune -a`)
   -> only auto-heal the safe class; rescue-before-delete; default to report/dry-run.
5. "Fix" that only prints links (RN `--fix`) -> don't market advise-only as autofix.
6. Prerequisite/ordering cascades (docker DDxxxx) -> short-circuit dependents on a
   failed root check instead of emitting a confusing cascade.

Prior art surveyed: brew doctor, flutter doctor, react-native doctor (richest
per-check autofix model — `HealthCheckInterface` with `getDiagnostics` +
`runAutomaticFix`), npm doctor, yarn doctor, gh auth status, rustup (cautionary — no
doctor exists), docker diagnose, git fsck vs git maintenance (sharpest report-vs-mutate
line), terraform validate/fmt, chezmoi doctor (best severity vocabulary).

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] `rebar doctor` runs a registry of category-tagged checks with crash-isolation and per-check timeouts
- [ ] Auto-heals only the provably-safe class (the migration ensure-registry); advises everything else with an exact next-step command
- [ ] Severity tiers (ok/info/warning/error/failed + healed); exit code gates on the fatal tier only; warnings never fail; behavior is tested
- [ ] `--check`/`--dry-run` read-only mode (CI gate) and `--json` machine output, both with a tested exit-code contract
- [ ] All four categories covered: migration drift (auto-heal), store integrity (reuse fsck), config consistency, environment/dependencies
- [ ] Resolve `upgrade` command relationship (alias vs migration-only subset)
- [ ] Depends on the migration-pattern epic (ensure-registry + version marker) as the auto-heal substrate

## Discovered from bug 9f63 (Step 7 construct sweep)

Same defect class as 9f63 — **a persisted position advanced on "seen" rather than "done"** — but here the lost artifact is observability data rather than a work item.

`infra/scripts/observability.sh:208-212` (and the same shape at `:104`/`:107-108` replication, `:134`/`:137-138` voter, `:157`/`:158` merge-change, `:178`/`:179` deploy):

```sh
new=$((total - prev))
[ "$new" -lt 0 ] && new=$total
echo "$total" >"$offset_file"          # <-- offset advances FIRST
aws cloudwatch put-metric-data ... --value "$new" 2>/dev/null || true   # <-- may fail, silently
```

The offset file is written **before** the publish, and the publish is `2>/dev/null || true`. A transient failure (CloudWatch throttle, IMDS credential blip, network) therefore loses that interval's delta permanently: the next tick computes `total - prev` from the already-advanced baseline, so the count is never re-published.

**Loss is permanent, not self-healing** — unlike a rotation cursor, this offset excludes rather than deprioritizes.

## Why it matters more than it looks

The `voter_errors` metric is what alarms on a broken `LLM-Review` gate. So a `voter_errors` spike that happens to coincide with a CloudWatch hiccup goes un-alarmed forever — the exact "the failure is invisible" property that made 9f63 so expensive to diagnose, in the mechanism that is supposed to be watching it.

## Fix sketch

Invert the order at each of the five sites: publish first, advance the offset only when `put-metric-data` exits 0. On failure leave the offset alone so the next tick re-publishes a cumulative delta (over-reporting once is strictly safer than silently under-reporting forever).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] At each of the five offset sites the offset is written only after a successful publish
- [ ] A failed publish leaves the offset unchanged, proven by a test that stubs a failing `aws` and asserts the offset file is byte-identical afterwards
- [ ] A subsequent successful publish reports the accumulated delta, not just the latest tick

## Idea: Human-in-the-loop (HITL) approval gate the agent cannot self-satisfy

### Problem

rebar's start-work and completion gates are enforced in-process by the same runtime the
agent drives, and their escape hatches are reachable by the agent itself. In particular,
`rebar review-plan --force` bypasses the plan-review claim gate, and it is CLI-invocable by an
autonomous agent. Recent real-world drift (session `5eb0` / epic `708d`): an agent, acting on a
vague human instruction, rationalized repeated `--force` plan reviews of blocked tickets rather
than deferring — each individually plausible, collectively defeating the gate's intent (mint no
signed attestation against not-yet-final dependencies). 2026 research frames this precisely:

- *Ambig-DS* (arXiv 2605.09698) — under-specified tasks produce **silent commitments** to
  plausible-but-unintended framings; the bottleneck is recognizing underspecification.
- *Bayesian and Motivated Reasoning in AI Agents* (arXiv 2608.00339) — framing/priors
  "neither specified in the task nor visible in the decision record" silently drive conclusions.
- *Securing Agentic AI: From Per-Action Checks to Trajectory Assurance* (arXiv 2608.01558) —
  "sequences of individually permissible actions may collectively violate system-level
  constraints"; safety must be a **verifiable property of the runtime**, not "an optional
  layer of guidance."

The common thread: any approval an agent can *produce* it can *rationalize producing*. A robust
HITL gate must be one the agent structurally **cannot replicate**, only *request*.

### Proposed direction (to be designed via the brainstorm protocol before any build)

Add a HITL approval primitive to rebar that gates a configurable set of consequential /
policy-overriding operations (initial candidates: `review-plan --force`, force-close, limit
changes to `.github/module-size-limit.txt`, and any future `--force` escape hatch) behind an
approval token that:

1. **Is unforgeable by the agent** — the approval is bound to a secret/authority the agent has
   no access to. Sketches to evaluate (prior-art review required, per the brainstorm skill's
   "interrogate novelty" step): a detached signature over the request payload made with a key
   held only by a human/CI identity (mirroring the existing plan-review attestation signing but
   with a *separate, agent-inaccessible* key); a Gerrit-style out-of-band vote by a
   non-agent account; a one-time approval nonce minted by a human-operated command.
2. **Is request/grant-separated** — the agent can only emit a *request* (payload = operation,
   target ticket(s), reason, base SHA). Granting happens in a channel the agent cannot drive;
   the agent then presents the returned token, which rebar verifies against the
   agent-inaccessible authority before allowing the operation.
3. **Is bound and non-replayable** — the token is scoped to the exact operation + target +
   content hash + a short expiry, so a grant for one action cannot be reused for another
   (defeats the "series of individually-plausible forces" pattern; cf. trajectory assurance).
4. **Fails closed and is auditable** — absent/invalid/expired/stale token → operation refused;
   every request and grant is recorded as ticket/session-log events for the decision record
   (directly answering the "not visible in the decision record" finding).

### Explicitly OUT of scope for the primitive itself
- Replacing the existing signing/attestation machinery (this *complements* it with an authority
  the agent cannot hold).
- Deciding *which* operations require HITL — that policy surface is a follow-on decision; this
  idea establishes the mechanism and a minimal initial op set.

### Why an idea, not an open ticket
This needs a full brainstorm pass (purpose / problem / edge cases / implementation) and a
prior-art review (existing human-approval / four-eyes / signing-authority patterns, and why
OSS agent frameworks do or don't gate self-escalation) before it is claimable work. Promote
`idea -> open` and author child stories once the design is settled and the plan-review gate can
be satisfied.

### Acceptance criteria (for the eventual design, not this idea)
- A documented threat model showing the agent cannot mint a valid approval token by any
  in-process or CLI path available to it.
- The gated operation set is config-driven and fails closed.
- Request + grant + verification are recorded as durable, queryable events.

## Premise validation: a BEHAVIOUR-PRESERVING `reconcile_one` is not available

Validated the goal against current `origin/main` (cc69cc1179) plus the in-flight change for
`envious-metal-budgie` (Gerrit 1665), which rewrites the doctor's fold. Two independent passes
(mine and a held-out analysis) reach the same conclusion: sync and the S3 doctor agree on about
four lines of graph arithmetic and disagree on every policy that matters. The ticket's AC #1
("no duplicated merge/unrelated-history logic") cannot be met without policy flags that flip
safety-critical branches.

### The blocking divergences

1. **Unrelated-history policy is CONTRADICTORY, not merely different.** `sync._do_reconverge`
   REFUSES and mutates nothing when there is no common ancestor and the local store already
   carries events (`sync.py:144-152`, predicate `_carries_ticket_events` at `sync.py:80-104`) —
   its documented purpose is to avoid grafting an orphan store into the shared tickets branch.
   The doctor UNIONS unconditionally (`s3_doctor.py` fold), and that is pinned by a held-out
   test on a non-empty tracker: `test_s3_doctor_heldout.py:81-103`
   (`REDACTED_TOKEN`, asserting "unrelated head discarded" must not
   happen). The same input shape must produce opposite outcomes. A shared
   `allow_unrelated=` parameter would be a safety-critical policy flag, not a knob.

2. **The merge MECHANISM cannot be unified without breaking sync.** After 1665 the doctor folds
   with `merge-tree --write-tree` + `commit-tree` and deliberately never touches the worktree.
   Sync cannot do that: its consumers read ticket events off the tracker's WORKTREE FILES
   (`_engine_support/reads.py:296,312` -> `reducer/_api.py:127-176`, which scans event files off
   disk and caches to `<ticket_dir>/.cache.json`). A ref-only merge would advance the ref while
   readers kept seeing pre-merge state — silent staleness. Sync is always the checked-out case,
   so it can only ever use the `git merge` / `reset --hard` shape.

3. **Failure policy is opposed.** Sync must never raise: `_union_merge` aborts, keeps local and
   logs a warning (`sync.py:191-196`), and its read path wraps `reconverge` in a bare
   `except Exception: pass` (`_engine_support/reads.py:253-258`). The doctor must raise —
   `push_classify.py:189-201` catches `S3DoctorConflict`, logs `exc.hint`, escalates under
   `strict`, and abandons the push.

4. **Epoch guard asymmetry.** Sync pins the remote ref and refuses across incompatible store
   epochs via `compat.store_epoch_merge_target` (`sync.py:177-180`). The doctor has no analog
   and never reads `.store-compat.json`; its heads are immutable `refs/rebar-doctor/<sha>`
   scratch refs, so only the pinning half is covered incidentally. Adding the guard is a new
   refusal branch; dropping it is a safety regression.

5. **Cardinality and lock scope differ.** Sync reconciles ONE remote head against HEAD under a
   lock covering the whole decision (timeout 15, plain `run_git`); the doctor folds N heads with
   an unborn-tip seeding rule, fetches bundles OUTSIDE the lock, and locks only the fold
   (timeout 30, `run_git_write`). The doctor's lock placement is pinned by
   `test_s3_doctor_heldout.py:205`.

### What is actually shareable

Only a classification helper — `merge_class(tip, head) -> ANCESTOR | UNRELATED | DIVERGED`,
absorbing two git probes from each side (`sync.py:144,163` and the doctor's equivalents). That
is roughly four lines of shared surface, and both call sites would still own their merge,
publish, refusal and failure logic.

### Options for the operator

- **(A) Close as obsolete.** The duplication this ticket targeted was the doctor's copy of the
  worktree `git merge` policy. After 1665 the doctor no longer has a worktree merge at all, so
  the thing to de-duplicate is gone.
- **(B) Thin share only.** Extract `merge_class` and nothing else. Honest but low-value; it
  trades four duplicated lines for a new cross-module dependency between the store's two most
  safety-critical healers.
- **(C) Deep unification.** Genuinely possible, but NOT behaviour-preserving: it requires
  deciding the contradictory unrelated-history policy, moving sync onto a merge-tree engine plus
  an explicit worktree sync, and reconciling raise-vs-warn. That is a rewrite of the store's
  hottest path and needs its own ticket and plan.

Recommending (A), with (B) as a defensible second. Not proceeding without a scope decision,
because every path that satisfies AC #1 as written is behaviour-changing.

## Summary
Whitespace-only changes to a ticket description invalidate its signed plan-review attestation, forcing an unnecessary (slow, costly) re-review before the close gate will accept the ticket.

## Repro (observed this session on 28cd-d8f8-4456-482c)
1. A ticket has a certified/signed plan review at description length 7098 chars (ending in a single trailing newline).
2. Re-set the description via `rebar edit --description="$(cat file)"` — shell command substitution strips the trailing newline, so the stored description becomes 7097 chars. The visible content is byte-identical apart from that one trailing \n.
3. `rebar review-plan <id> --status` returns `{"ok": false, "verdict": "stale-material", "reason": "the plan was materially edited since review — changed: description (7098 -> 7097 chars)"}`.
4. `rebar transition <id> in_progress closed` is blocked by the plan-review close gate with 'stale-material' and demands a fresh `review-plan`.

Note (contrast): ticking acceptance-criteria checkboxes (`- [ ]` -> `- [x]`) is correctly hash-invisible and does NOT invalidate the review. Only the insignificant-whitespace delta (a trailing newline) drifted the material fingerprint.

## Expected
Plan-review material canonicalization should normalize insignificant whitespace before hashing so that whitespace-only edits — trailing/leading newline differences, trailing spaces on a line, and analogous no-semantic-change edits — do not invalidate a signed plan review or trip the stale-material close gate. Only semantically meaningful description changes should drift the material.

## Impact
An operator ticking ACs and re-saving a description (a routine close-time step, and one where CLI $(...) newline-stripping is easy to hit) can be forced into a full LLM re-review (~7-15 min + model spend) purely for a trailing-newline difference. This wastes gate budget and slows the close path, and risks tempting a --force bypass.

## Suggested fix direction
In the plan-review material builder (the description material-part hash, currently reported like 'description <hash> <char-count>'), apply a canonicalization pass (e.g. strip trailing whitespace per line + normalize trailing newlines to a single canonical form, consistent with how AC-checkbox state is already normalized out) before fingerprinting. ## Three content-DESTROYING pandoc behaviours a real-prose corpus caught
All measured on pandoc 3.6.1 (the binary bundled in the `pypandoc-binary==1.15` wheel), rendering `-f commonmark -t jira --wrap=none`. Each one silently corrupts content, and none is visible from hand-written examples:

1. **pandoc escapes punctuation INSIDE code spans.** `` `-> <- <-> =>` `` renders as `{{\-> <\- <-> =>}}`. Pre-substituting arrows correctly spares code, and pandoc corrupts it anyway on the way out. A "skip code when substituting" rule alone is NOT sufficient.
2. **pandoc DELETES HTML comments.** A lone `<!-- rebar:reconciler-echo -->` renders to the EMPTY STRING. That is rebar's own reconciler echo marker, so this is a correctness bug, not a cosmetic one — a dropped marker breaks loop-breaking.
3. **A naive arrow rule corrupts the HTML-comment terminator.** `-->` contains `->`, so substitution rewrites it to `-→`. Fix: match `<!--` and `-->` FIRST and map them to themselves so the inner arrow is consumed by the delimiter.

Mitigation that covers all three without enumerating pandoc's quirks: a **post-render code-preservation check** — after converting a unit, require every code fragment of the source to appear verbatim in the output, else fall back to that unit's original Markdown. This converts unpredictable escaping into a safe fallback. Recommend adding it whatever the implementation shape.

Also worth keeping: pandoc's jira writer emits a stray `{anchor:}` after EVERY heading (`h1. {anchor:}Title`) — it is not content and needs stripping; and re-rendering already-wiki text as Markdown is destructive (`{{x}}` → `\{\{x\}\}`, `{noformat}` dissolves), so a unit that already looks like wiki should pass through.

## The cutover must tolerate a no-extras install
Story e59d ships the Cloud Markdown↔ADF functions with **marklas (plus its transitive mistune) as a pinned OPTIONAL EXTRA, lazily imported inside the three function bodies, with `ImportError` routed to the existing plain-text `adf.py` fallback.** It is NOT vendored.

The lazy-import extra is the only option preserving that contract, and it mirrors the `agents`/`metrics`/`grounding` precedents.

**Consequence this story owns:** in an install without the extra, `adf.markdown_to_adf` / `adf_to_markdown` / `fit_markdown_to_adf_limit` return their PLAIN `adf.py` results. So the cutover — which repoints `AdfCodec`'s four ops and the live Cloud send/fit/compare sites — must behave correctly when the Markdown-aware path is silently unavailable, i.e. it degrades to today's plain-text ADF behaviour rather than raising or emitting a half-converted wire.
